How it works and where it comes from: [Sound 27: Ambient music](../lessons/sound-ambient.qmd).

## Generator

<div class="sk" data-w="ambient" data-preset="Airport (tape loops)"></div>

**Energy** is one knob that moves many settings at once, like the Super Knob on a Yamaha MODX. The table under it shows each one: where it starts (From, which is wherever that setting was when Energy was last at 0), where it ends up at full Energy (To, which you can type), and where it is now. As you turn Energy up, the loops get busier and faster, the echo feeds back towards the edge, drive turns the noise and bells to grit, and cymbal swells and chimes pile up. A limiter stops it all from running away. Untick a row to leave that setting alone.

**Changes: Cued** holds back what you change while it plays. The slider shows the new value but the sound keeps the old one until you press **Go**. Then every cued setting glides to its new value over the **Transition** time, the way a DJ or a live-electronics player moves from one scene to the next. Scale, key, instrument and the loops' shape change at the start of the glide. Turning Energy while cued works the same way. The **Wind chimes** menu sets up the chime tubes, which are modelled, not recorded: how they're tuned (to the generator's key), how long the longest tube is (bass, baritone or tenor), how hard the striker is, how long they ring, how loud and how wide. The **Cymbal swells** menu chooses which of the Drum Kits' cymbal recordings play, how loud, how fast, how wide and how many play backwards. **Loop notes on** can also play modelled church bells (still being worked on), Korean and Japanese temple bells, bass bars (metal or wood) or chime tubes. None of these are recordings. Each is built from its partials, using published measurements of real instruments where there are any.

**Loops** gives each tape loop its own instrument and octave. One choice is the **Drone voice**: the drone's own sound (detuned saws or the scanned wavetable), played as a note with its own attack, hold and release, set in the Drone voice menu. **Loop octave** moves every loop up or down. **Church bell type** chooses which real bell the church-bell model follows: a modern tuned bell (Westminster Abbey, Taylor, Eijsbouts) or an older one (1591, 1615, 1679, 1859), whose partials sit further from the ideal.

**LFOs** work as they do in the Vital synth: three very slow shapes, each one cycle every few seconds up to ten minutes. Each moves something: the drone filters, the wavetable scan, the brightness, the drone or noise level, the echo, the reverb or the drone voice's pan. Two aimed at the same thing add up, so the movement never quite repeats. The plot shows the last minute.

**Stop** has three settings. **Hard stop** stops everything at once. **Gradual stop** winds everything down to silence over the Wind-down time, then lets the reverb and the rings finish before it really stops. **Stop and ring** adds nothing new from the moment you press it: the drone and noise fade in two seconds, and whatever is ringing plays out. While it winds down, press the button again to stop at once.

**● Record take** records what you hear for up to five minutes, then **Open in the DAW** opens it in the [DAW scratch pad](daw.qmd) as a new project. You get one note track per tape loop, so you can see the loops drifting apart on the piano roll. You also get an audio track for what you heard (Master) and one for each part: loop notes, chimes, cymbals, drone, noise, reverb and echo. Solo a part to hear it alone. Each setting you changed gets its own muted track, whose volume line shows the setting over time.

## Bells, chimes and bass bars

The instruments the generator can use, on their own. **Strike** plays one note; **▶ Play** lets each one play by itself: the bell tolls, the chime tubes play gusts on a pentatonic set, the bars play a bass pattern. All of them are built from their partials, not recorded. The chime tube and the bars follow published measurements. The temple bells follow measurements of the Divine Bell of King Seongdeok (Korea) and the Mii-dera bell (Japan): struck by a wooden log, with a slow beat from pairs of nearly equal partials. No Vietnamese bell has been measured, so for now it uses the Japanese model, which is the closest in shape. The church bell is still being worked on.

## Works Cited

<!-- works-cited: written by scripts/works-cited.py -->
::: {.works-cited}
"Bronze Bells in Le-Nguyen Dynasty in the Vietnam National Museum of History." Vietnam National Museum of History. Vietnamese temple bells: cylindrical body, square shoulder, flaring mouth, two-dragon handle, four lotus striking knobs.

Cho, Wan-Ho, et al. "Reconstruction of the Spatial Radiation Characteristics of Large Korean Bell." <i>Forum Acusticum 2023</i>, pp. 2857-60. Doublet pairs of the King Seongdeok bell (Table 1): 168.3 (0.08 Hz), 190.1 (1.26), 228.3 (0.32), 282.6 (0.66), cluster 346-350 Hz.

"Composite Marimba Bars." US Patent 4,411,187. Marimba decay about 2 s at C3 to 1/50 s at C7; vibraphone 30 s at the low end to about 6 s at the high end.

Hibbert, Bill. "Identifying Bell Partials." hibberts.co.uk. Doublet 831.7 / 832.3 Hz on a 528 kg service bell.

Hibbert, Bill. "The Musical Sound Quality of Church Bells." hibberts.co.uk. The tierce is often the loudest partial; the quint is typically very quiet.

Hibbert, Bill. "The Tuning of Westminster Abbey Tenor." hibberts.co.uk. Church-bell partials in cents from the nominal: hum -2397, prime -1198, tierce -904, quint -498, superquint +699, octave nominal +1254, I-7..I-10.

Hite, Lee. "Design Decisions." leehite.org. Strike the end for most overtones; dead centre misses the first overtone; metal strikers give more overtones, softer ones a cleaner tone.

Hite, Lee. <i>Tubular Bell Chimes: Do-It-Yourself Compendium</i>. 2022. Free-free tube ratios x2.76, 5.40, 8.93, 13.34, 18.64 (p. 56); sustain mainly the fundamental, 1st overtone about 2 s for a 2-inch aluminium chime at 272.5 Hz (p. 57); a C2 chime sounds about like C5 (pp. 15-16); hang point 22.42% (pp. 26, 56).

Kim, Yang-Hann, and Sea-Moon Kim. "An Analysis of the Sound Radiation Characteristics of the King Song-Dok Bell Using Cylindrical Acoustic Holography." <i>Journal of the Acoustical Society of Korea</i>, vol. 16, no. 4, 1997, pp. 94-100. Hum doublet 64.06 / 64.38 Hz, beat about 3 s; energy even up to 800 Hz at the strike; after about 10 s only the 64 Hz pair is left.

Kim, Yeon-mi, and Sungeun Lee. "Acoustic Study of the Sacred Bell of King Seongdeok." <i>ISPRS Archives</i>, vol. XLVIII-M-9-2025, 2025, pp. 735-40 (title as listed in a search; to check). Hum split 0.32-0.37 Hz, beat 2.94 s; 168 Hz pair split 0.10-0.13 Hz; the beat strength depends on direction.

Kirkby, David. "Physics of Music, Lecture 14." University of California, Irvine. Mallet contact time T damps frequencies above about 2/T; vibraphone 1:4; resonators reinforce odd harmonics.

McCarthy, Jim. "Marimbas: Exploring the Depths." Percussion Clinic Adelaide, 1994. Overtones 1 and 2 decay in about 1/2 and 1/7 of the fundamental's time (Bork and Meyer); a low resonator takes about 0.7 s to build up.

Rau, Mark, Orchisama Das, and Elliot K. Canfield-Dafilou. "Improved Carillon Synthesis." <i>Proceedings of DAFx-19</i>, 2019. C3 carillon bell: low modes ring about 100 s (fig. 3b); clapper contact 1-1.4 ms; louder strikes brighter at 1.5-3 kHz.

Rossing, Thomas D., Junehee Yoo, and Andrew Morrison. "Acoustics of Percussion Instruments: An Update." <i>Acoustical Science and Technology</i>, vol. 25, no. 6, 2004, pp. 406-412. Marimba bars tuned 1:4:10 (the 4th harmonic held for the first 3-3.5 octaves, the 10th for 2).

Sakurai, Naoki, et al. "Nihon no bonsho no bubun'on to shindo modo ni tsuite" [Partials and vibration modes of Japanese temple bells]. <i>Ningen Kankyo Kagaku</i>, vol. 27, 2020, pp. 3-13. Mii-dera bell partials 109, 216, 253, 320/323, 350, 409, 466/477, 567 Hz; a weak 47 Hz mode inside the bell; at 13 s only 109 and 216 Hz remain.
:::
